newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Bombay getting back to basics.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bombay getting back to basics.

text.p: Cutting short a costly flirtation with young and trendy customers, Bombay Co Inc aims to regain its stride in a year or so by refocusing on the antique reproduction furniture with which it made its name, new Chief Executive Officer Carson Thompson said.

"It is going to take us five months to reposition our inventory, and it takes usually at least six months to get a new product stream started. And it takes beyond that then to get completely on track," Thompson said in an interview with Reuters. "This is not a few-day turnaround."

One week after former Wall Street darlings Robert and Alexandra Nourse were ousted from the company's management team, Thompson said getting back to basics was central to the Fort Worth-based furniture retailer's turnaround bid.

He said the Nourses had tried to be "too upscale, too fashionable" with an eclectic line of light woods and metals, and had neglected to bring in new models for its traditional line of mahogany, cherry and other darkwood desks and tables.
"To a significant extent they just vacated our mainstream business that is an extremely important part of the company," Thompson said.
"What we are doing here now is refocusing on the core Bombay business with the known strategies that have worked historically," he said.
That means turning back to Bombay's core customers -- women in their 40s, with children and a household income of about $70,000.
Bombay's sales and profits surged in the early 1990s. With the Nourse husband-and-wife team winning glowing tributes from industry analysts, its stock jumped to more than $30 a share in early 1994.
Since then, profit margins have shrunk and the share price has plummeted back down to around $6.

Thompson said the collapse can be easily explained. An inadequate number of new products meant the company had to offer "excessive" promotional sales in order to keep revenues coming in. That hurt margins and shortened the life-cycle of product lines, exacerbating the problem of new models.
In the six months ended August 3, Bombay's chain of 431 stores recorded a net loss of $4.8 million, or $0.12 a share, on lower revenues of $139 million.
Thompson said the company would also lose money in its third quarter. It would rebound briefly during the Christmas season and then show losses again in the first half of 1997.

But he was optimistic that once new lines were introduced for Bombay's traditional customers, it would be able to reduce promotional sales, restore margins and post steady profits in the last six months of 1997 and beyond.
He said Bombay was currently testing two pilot stores in outlet malls and would probably begin over the next nine to 15 months to consider opening stores abroad, notably in Japan, Britain and France.
